definition: A deliberately distorted representation that becomes recognizable from a particular viewpoint or through an optical device, making the conditions of viewing essential to how an image coheres as an intelligible form.
etymology: From Greek-derived elements associated with forming again or transformation, transmitted through learned European terminology for deliberately distorted, reconstructable optical representations.
tagline: Recognition has an address in space
art_caption: An elongated lattice projects into a coherent circular form along one privileged axis.

sections.heading: A distortion with a rule
sections.text: An anamorphic image is deliberately transformed so that a particular viewpoint or optical device restores its recognizable form. A pavement painting may look stretched from above yet convincing from a marked position. The apparent disorder follows a designed projection, making the viewer's location an operative part of the representation.

sections.heading: Two families of reconstruction
sections.text: Perspective anamorphosis uses a specially positioned eye, while mirror anamorphosis can require a cylindrical or conical reflecting surface. The procedures differ geometrically, but both link distorted marks to a mode of reconstruction. Neither is adequately described as discovering a familiar shape in arbitrary noise or cloud patterns.

sections.heading: Ordinary perspective made strange
sections.text: Anamorphosis dramatizes a condition that ordinary pictures often conceal: coherence depends on relations between image, surface, and viewpoint. The privileged position is constructed rather than naturally inevitable. Moving away from it makes that dependence visible, allowing a viewer to experience both a recognizable object and the means of its recognition.

sections.heading: Change position before interpretation
sections.text: Imagine a stretched oval laid across a floor. Ask which oblique viewpoint would make it appear circular, then compare that prediction with a simple physical model. The exercise links visual surprise to geometry. A metaphor about changed understanding becomes sharper when this dependence on a determinate viewing relation is preserved.

literary: From the doorway it was wreckage; from the last stair, a face, and he learned how fiercely a truth may depend upon the inch of floor beneath it.
